item.title: PMs face limits

item.content:encoded:
THE Daniel Fatiaki led electoral review report had proposed introducing term limits and a compulsory retirement age for Fiji’s prime minister, reveals the 232-page report, An Electoral System for the People, From the People. The report contained a roadmap of proposed constitutional and electoral changes.

Led by former chief justice Daniel Fatiaki, the commission was appointed in 2025 to review key election-related laws, including the Electoral Act 2014, the Electoral (Registration of Voters) Act 2012, and the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding & Disclosures) Act 2013. The Fiji Times understands this report has been superseded by the Constitution Review Report – compiled by the seven-member Constitution Review Commission that was appointed in March 2026 this year to review the 2013 Constitution. The CRC report was considered by Cabinet last week and will go to Parliament soon.

Among the proposals in the report, that has been obtained by The Fiji Times, was the introduction of constitutional limits on the tenure of the prime minister and a compulsory retirement age. The document states the prime minister should be permitted to serve two terms and retire at the age of 75.

It also proposed constitutional rules governing the early announcement of election dates and provisions for a caretaker government.

Another recommendation sought to prevent changes to electoral laws from taking effect in the year before the last possible date for a general election unless the Electoral Commission determined that the changes could be implemented without undue risk to the integrity of the election.

The earlier report also proposed removing detailed electoral provisions from the Constitution and placing them in electoral legislation while retaining broad electoral principles in the Constitution.

It recommended a mixed-member proportional electoral system combining local constituencies, a closed national party list and constituencies reserved for women.

The proposed model would retain 71 MPs and reduce the threshold for parties to qualify for national list seats from five per cent to two per cent.

Other proposals included establishing a Constituency Boundaries Commission and an appointed, apolitical Senate.

item.title: FSC ramps up harvesting
item.description: THE Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) has accelerated harvesting efforts before the impact of the prolonged dry spell impacts harvesting and replanting campaigns for the 2027 crushing season. Board chairperson Nitya Reddy said the corporation’s immediate focus was on maximising sugar recovery from every tonne of cane delivered as they anticipate a reduction in cane availability.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC) has accelerated harvesting efforts before the impact of the prolonged dry spell impacts harvesting and replanting campaigns for the 2027 crushing season.

Board chairperson Nitya Reddy said the corporation’s immediate focus was on maximising sugar recovery from every tonne of cane delivered as they anticipate a reduction in cane availability.

“This includes maturity-based, or Brix-based, harvesting to ensure that cane is harvested at the optimum stage of maturity,” he said.

“A number of operational and logistical measures are also being implemented across the mills.

“FSC is accelerating the conversion from manual to mechanical harvesting, with a target of approximately 100,000 tonnes across three mills, including 40,000 tonnes at Labasa Mill.

“This is intended to facilitate faster harvesting before the impact of the drought intensifies.”

He said harvester logistics were being prioritised to reach cane in distant sectors as well as hilly and sloping areas that are particularly vulnerable to drought.

“FSC is working to reduce crop stand-over across the three mills to less than 20,000 tonnes, with the objective of harvesting as much of the available crop as possible.

“At Labasa, 16 harvesting gangs from Corrections Department, involving 166 cutters, are currently engaged, the highest level to date.

“The target is to harvest approximately 11,000 tonnes at Labasa Mill, which is about double last year’s level.”

Mr Reddy added FSC would continue to provide a $5 per tonne subsidy for manual harvesting, increased from $3 per tonne last year.

“At Labasa, the number of cage bins in operation has been increased to a record 60, supporting growers in the Daku-Wainikoro sectors.

“This has enabled cane supply through the cage-bin system to be increased from approximately 4000 tonnes to 8000 tonnes.

“These measures are aimed at reducing harvesting delays, improving the flow of cane to the mills and maximising sugar production despite the anticipated decline in overall cane supply.”

item.title: Park rehab plan
item.description: The Suva City Council is considering new measures to improve the condition of Albert Park, with a renewed focus on grass maintenance and rehabilitation. Council chairman and acting CEO Tevita Boseiwaqa said strategies were being considered to help the grass recover, including conservation, regular maintenance and limiting access to the grounds in certain circumstances.
item.content:encoded:
The Suva City Council is considering new measures to improve the condition of Albert Park, with a renewed focus on grass maintenance and rehabilitation.

Council chairman and acting CEO Tevita Boseiwaqa said strategies were being considered to help the grass recover, including conservation, regular maintenance and limiting access to the grounds in certain circumstances.

He said the council was also reviewing previous work carried out at the park to determine what could be improved.

Plans include the use of manure to encourage grass growth, while damaged sections of the playing areas could be replanted using grass plugs.

Mr Boseiwaqa said funding had been allocated specifically towards the maintenance of Albert Park, but he did not disclose the amount.

He said the funding would support ongoing upkeep as the council worked to establish healthier and more durable grass.

A special type of grass is also being considered as part of the rehabilitation plans.

Albert Park remains an important public space, hosting sporting activities, community gatherings and major events throughout the year.

item.title: Minister yet to see results
item.description: EDUCATION Minister Aseri Radrodro says he cannot comment on Fiji’s 2025 literacy and numeracy results because he has yet to see the national report. “I’ve yet to see the report,” Mr Radrodro said.
item.content:encoded:
EDUCATION Minister Aseri Radrodro says he cannot comment on Fiji’s 2025 literacy and numeracy results because he has yet to see the national report.

“I’ve yet to see the report,” Mr Radrodro said.

“When I’ll see the report, then I can comment on it.”

His comments come as new Pacific-wide assessment results highlight serious concerns over primary school literacy, with 46 per cent of Year 6 students performing at or below the Year 4 reading benchmark.

The Pacific Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (PILNA) 2025 Regional Report covering 15 countries, found only 44 per cent of Year 4 learners met minimum reading proficiency.

Pacific Community deputy director Seci Waqabaca said it did not contain results from Fiji because this was not shared.

The regional report identified reading as the Pacific’s biggest education challenge and called for a comprehensive response.

item.title: 25 seats proposed for women – report
item.description: THE Daniel Fatiaki led Electoral Review Commission had recommended that women get at least 35 per cent representation in Parliament under a major electoral reform proposal recommending 25 constituencies reserved exclusively for female candidates. The proposal is contained in the 232-page report, An Electoral System for the People, From the People, produced by the electoral law reform commission an
item.content:encoded:
THE Daniel Fatiaki led Electoral Review Commission had recommended that women get at least 35 per cent representation in Parliament under a major electoral reform proposal recommending 25 constituencies reserved exclusively for female candidates.

The proposal is contained in the 232-page report, An Electoral System for the People, From the People, produced by the electoral law reform commission and obtained by The Fiji Times.

Led by former chief justice Daniel Fatiaki, the commission was appointed in 2025 to review key election-related laws, including the Electoral Act 2014, the Electoral (Registration of Voters) Act 2012, and the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding & Disclosures) Act 2013. The Fiji Times understands this report has been superseded by the Constitution Review Report – compiled by the seven-member Constitution Review Commission that was appointed in March 2026 this year to review the 2013 Constitution. The CRC report was considered by Cabinet last week and will go to Parliament soon.

Under the proposed system, Parliament would retain 71 seats, with 25 reserved seats for women. While only women would be eligible to contest these constituencies, both men and women would vote for the candidates.

The commissioners describe the proposal as a “radical ‘first’” for Fiji’s electoral system.

They say the arrangement would provide women with about 35 per cent of parliamentary representation, exceeding the target under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).

The review also considered requiring political parties to meet quotas for female candidates but concluded that quotas alone may not address the disadvantages women face during election campaigns.

It also proposed boundaries for the 25 reserved constituencies that would match those of other local constituencies to minimise confusion.

The report also suggests male and female candidates could campaign as teams, potentially providing women with greater logistical support and security. If accepted, this would mark a significant shift from Fiji’s current system, where women compete directly with men for parliamentary seats without gender-reserved constituencies.

item.title: TSLS tightens rules for failing students
item.description: TERTIARY students who repeatedly fail to meet academic requirements will face tougher consequences under new TSLS rules, with allowances cut for those placed on second probation and scholarship support withdrawn for those suspended. Education Minister Aseri Radrodro said students on first probation would continue receiving their normal allowances, but those placed on second probation would have th
item.content:encoded:
TERTIARY students who repeatedly fail to meet academic requirements will face tougher consequences under new TSLS rules, with allowances cut for those placed on second probation and scholarship support withdrawn for those suspended.

Education Minister Aseri Radrodro said students on first probation would continue receiving their normal allowances, but those placed on second probation would have their allowances stopped, with only tuition fees covered.

“However, if placed on a second probation, students will no longer receive allowances and only their tuition fees will be covered,” Mr Radrodro said at the launch of the 2027 TSLS Scholarship Policies Handbook in Suva yesterday.

Students suspended after two consecutive probations will receive neither tuition nor allowances and must continue their studies privately until they demonstrate that they meet the required academic standard.

“These measures are intended to promote discipline, improve completion rates, and ensure that Government investment must show the value for money.”

At the same time, the Government has raised the academic threshold for its revamped Hardship Assistance Scheme from a 50 per cent pass to a 67 per cent cumulative GPA.

Mr Radrodro said the scheme would provide 500 awards for students who have privately completed one year of full-time study.

“The entry requirement has now changed from a 50 per cent pass to a 67 per cent cumulative GPA.”

He said student allowances would also be paid in at least four instalments instead of two to encourage better financial management.

Mr Radrodro urged scholarship recipients to take their studies seriously.

“You are fortunate to get a scholarship. You must show your gratitude to the people and the country by serving the local workforce, at least during your bonding period.”

item.title: Rape accused testifies
item.description: A FORMER Virgin Australia crew member was just looking for a safe escort back to her hotel after getting separated from friends on New Year’s Eve, the man accused or raping her told the High Court in Lautoka yesterday. Taking the stand on day four of his trial, Ilaisa Tanoa Degei denied allegations of rape and sexual assault, framing his actions as those of a helpful companion.
item.content:encoded:
A FORMER Virgin Australia crew member was just looking for a safe escort back to her hotel after getting separated from friends on New Year’s Eve, the man accused or raping her told the High Court in Lautoka yesterday.

Taking the stand on day four of his trial, Ilaisa Tanoa Degei denied allegations of rape and sexual assault, framing his actions as those of a helpful companion.

He recounted meeting the complainant at a nightclub in Nadi and after consuming a substantial amount of alcohol, he agreed to accompany the heavily intoxicated woman to a hotel.

He denied touching her, attempting to remove her clothing, or forcing her into a taxi, saying he merely intended to ensure her safe return.

State prosecutor Laisiasa Baleilevuka challenged this narrative during cross-examination and asked why he left his brother and friend behind at the club.

Mr Degei maintained they were simply friends who had just met.

The court heard that after stopping the taxi near the hotel junction, he went off to relieve himself.

Mr Degei told the court that he helped the complainant up by the waist and moments later, a police patrol intervened and brought both to the Namaka Police Station.

His brother testified that the complainant had initiated physical contact at the club by taking his brother’s hand and leading him out of the nighclub.

Justice Sunil Sharma adjourned the trial to September 18 for closing submissions.
